scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire cohort (n=92) consists of patients with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) recruited via a German occupational-disease pathway, stratified by whether they also meet Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a German clinical study of 92 patients with long-standing, severe post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), about half of whom also met criteria for ME/CFS, who were undergoing evaluation for occupational disability. Using cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), the authors found that most patients had objectively reduced oxygen uptake and power output, with 66.3% meeting thresholds the authors define as 'absolute work disability,' and that these objective measures correlated with patients' self-reported disability (Bell Disability Scale) and with their actual employment status (sick leave, reintegration, or working). The study documents functional/occupational burden (persistent symptoms averaging ~24 months, high post-exertional malaise prevalence, high rates of being on sick leave) but does not report any direct medical costs, indirect monetary costs, insurance payment amounts, or caregiver costs. It is a single-cohort clinical/occupational-medicine study, not a cost-of-illness analysis, and the cohort was deliberately selected for severity and occupational-disability referral, so its percentages should not be read as general-population PCC or ME/CFS burden estimates.

modeled_issues.issue: Objective work disability rate (CPET-defined: VO2peak < 15 mL/min/kg and/or PPO < 1 W/kg)
modeled_issues.population: Severely affected, long-standing PCC patients with suspected occupational disease, insured by German Social Accident Insurance (BGW), Mainz, Germany, recruited July 2023-March 2025

modeled_issues.issue: Prevalence of ME/CFS (Canadian Consensus Criteria) within this PCC cohort

modeled_issues.unit: % of cohort (71/92); 93% of ME/CFS subgroup vs 64% of non-ME/CFS subgroup, chi2=9.6, p=0.002

modeled_issues.issue: Proportion of cohort on medical sick leave due to PCC
modeled_issues.source_locator: Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10

modeled_issues.source_locator: Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10

modeled_issues.source_locator: Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10

modeled_issues.issue: Mean duration of persistent PCC symptoms
Pre-existing comorbidity prevalence and multimorbidity rate in cohort
modeled_issues.unit: % with at least one pre-existing disease (84/92); multimorbidity rate 42% (cohort's own figure, compared by the authors to 25.3% in cited age-matched general populations [46,47])
modeled_issues.source_locator: Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; Discussion, Clinical Profile, p.11

contextual_issues: Financial concerns, loan repayments, job loss, and the aspiration to contribute to society are mentioned (citing Lemogne & Pitron 2023) as factors motivating patients to continue working despite reduced physical capacity, but these are not quantified by this study.
Mental health and cognitive dysfunction are mentioned as additional factors limiting work ability beyond what CPET captures, but are not measured or quantified in this document.

All participants had initiated a formal procedure for official recognition of PCC as an occupational disease through the German Social Accident Insurance (BGW); this administrative/insurance-recognition burden is described but not quantified (e.g., no data on approval rates, wait times, or financial consequences of the process).
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost data (e.g., outpatient visits, hospitalizations, rehabilitation costs) are reported for this cohort, by ME/CFS status or otherwise.
No monetized indirect-cost data (lost wages, employer productivity loss, disability-insurance payouts) are reported, despite occupational status (sick leave/reintegration/working) being tracked.
No caregiver time, paid-help, or travel-cost data are reported anywhere in the document.
No healthy, age- and sex-matched control group was included, which the authors themselves note as a limitation affecting generalizability of the VO2peak/PPO findings.
No data on diagnostic delay, time-to-diagnosis, or repeated care-seeking history prior to study enrollment are reported.

No breakdown of any outcome (work disability rate, ME/CFS prevalence, PEM positivity, Bell-Score) by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status beyond ME/CFS classification, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status is reported, despite the cohort being 88% female.
No data on insurance claim outcomes (approval/denial, cost of occupational-disease recognition process) are reported.
comparison_boundaries: This cohort's ME/CFS prevalence (49%) must not be pooled with the 9.8%-15.4% prevalence the authors cite from other international PCC studies [9-11], because the authors themselves attribute the difference to recruitment bias toward severely affected, long-standing, occupationally disabled patients.

This cohort's multimorbidity rate (42%) must not be pooled with the 25.3% age-matched general-population rate cited from German/Swiss primary-care studies [46,47], as these represent different populations (occupational-disease-claim PCC cohort vs. general primary-care population) and possibly different multimorbidity definitions and measurement windows.

This cohort's VO2peak values (13.0-15.4 mL/min/kg in the severely affected occupational sample) must not be pooled with the population-based Peter et al. (2025) PCC-without-ME/CFS cohort (~27.9 mL/min/kg at 2 years post-infection), since these are structurally different populations (severity-selected occupational-disease claimants vs. a population-based sample), not alternate measurements of the same quantity.

All percentages and means reported here are specific to this single cohort (n=92, Mainz, Germany, enrolled July 2023-March 2025, 88% female, employed in healthcare/social-services sectors) and should not be extrapolated to the general PCC or ME/CFS population without an explicitly labeled assumption.

No dollar or cost figures of any kind appear in this document; nothing in it should be combined with cost data from other sources without separately establishing a matching price year, population, and cost perspective.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: Inclusion criterion 3 (Table 1) required that PCC diagnosis be established by a physician using ICD-10 code U09.9 as the main diagnosis; every patient in this cohort - and therefore every modeled_issues percentage derived from it (work disability rate, ME/CFS prevalence, PEM positivity, occupational status distribution, etc.) - was selected on the basis of already having received that diagnosis code, a claims/ICD-10-coded basis for cohort definition.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: Cohort-level percentages (66.3% objective work disability, 49% ME/CFS prevalence, 79% PEM positivity, 75%/12%/13% occupational status distribution, 48.9% Bell-Score ≤30) are each reported as a single pooled figure for the whole cohort, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status beyond ME/CFS classification, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, despite the cohort being 88% female.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a diagnostic/systemic gap in which organ-centered clinical diagnostics (cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurological) frequently yield unremarkable findings in severely affected PCC/ME-CFS patients, leaving clinicians without an objective framework to assess work ability, which the authors argue CPET is needed to fill.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Introduction states organ-centered clinical diagnostics 'frequently fail to explain their work disability' and that 'isolated, organ or system-specific assessments offer limited insight into global functional impairment'; the Conclusion states CPET 'guides further organ-centered clinical diagnostics' and enables individualized therapy and return-to-work decisions.

federal_evidence_used.how_used: Confirmed that U09.9 is the designated ICD-10-CM code for post-COVID-19 condition, used only to ground the claims_undercounting_caveat regarding this document's ICD-10 U09.9-based cohort inclusion criterion; not used to add any cost or prevalence figure.

decision_relevance.summary: This document supports occupational-medicine and disability-evaluation decisions for severely affected, long-standing PCC/ME-CFS patients rather than general cost-of-illness modeling, since it contains no dollar figures. Occupational physicians, workers'-compensation/disability insurers, and rehabilitation teams could use the reported CPET thresholds (VO2peak < 15 mL/min/kg, PPO < 1 W/kg) alongside the Bell Disability Scale to structure objective, non-organ-specific evaluations of work capacity. Patient advocates and clinicians could use the cohort's observed burden rates (66% objective work disability, 79% PEM positivity, 75% on sick leave) to illustrate functional burden within this specific severely-affected population, while researchers could use the explicit recruitment-bias and subgroup-disaggregation caveats to design better-stratified future PCC/ME-CFS cohorts.
use_cases: Occupational-disease evaluators and insurers (e.g., workers'-compensation assessors) could incorporate the CPET-derived VO2peak/PPO work-disability thresholds alongside subjective Bell-Score ratings into return-to-work and disability-determination protocols for severe PCC/ME-CFS, rather than relying on normal organ-centered test results alone.

Clinicians and rehabilitation teams could use the occupational-status stratification (sick leave vs. reintegration vs. working) and its association with VO2peak/PPO to counsel patients and plan individualized, graded return-to-work pathways.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire cohort (n=92) consists of patients with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) recruited via a German occupational-disease pathway, stratified by whether they also meet Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a German clinical study of 92 patients with long-standing, severe post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), about half of whom also met criteria for ME/CFS, who were undergoing evaluation for occupational disability. Using cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), the authors found that most patients had objectively reduced oxygen uptake and power output, with 66.3% meeting thresholds the authors define as 'absolute work disability,' and that these objective measures correlated with patients' self-reported disability (Bell Disability Scale) and with their actual employment status (sick leave, reintegration, or working). The study documents functional/occupational burden (persistent symptoms averaging ~24 months, high post-exertional malaise prevalence, high rates of being on sick leave) but does not report any direct medical costs, indirect monetary costs, insurance payment amounts, or caregiver costs. contextual_issues: Financial concerns, loan repayments, job loss, and the aspiration to contribute to society are mentioned (citing Lemogne & Pitron 2023) as factors motivating patients to continue working despite reduced physical capacity, but these are not quantified by this study.
Mental health and cognitive dysfunction are mentioned as additional factors limiting work ability beyond what CPET captures, but are not measured or quantified in this document.

All participants had initiated a formal procedure for official recognition of PCC as an occupational disease through the German Social Accident Insurance (BGW); this administrative/insurance-recognition burden is described but not quantified (e.g., no data on approval rates, wait times, or financial consequences of the process).
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost data (e.g., outpatient visits, hospitalizations, rehabilitation costs) are reported for this cohort, by ME/CFS status or otherwise.
No monetized indirect-cost data (lost wages, employer productivity loss, disability-insurance payouts) are reported, despite occupational status (sick leave/reintegration/working) being tracked.
No caregiver time, paid-help, or travel-cost data are reported anywhere in the document.
No healthy, age- and sex-matched control group was included, which the authors themselves note as a limitation affecting generalizability of the VO2peak/PPO findings.
No data on diagnostic delay, time-to-diagnosis, or repeated care-seeking history prior to study enrollment are reported.

No breakdown of any outcome (work disability rate, ME/CFS prevalence, PEM positivity, Bell-Score) by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status beyond ME/CFS classification, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status is reported, despite the cohort being 88% female.
No data on insurance claim outcomes (approval/denial, cost of occupational-disease recognition process) are reported.
comparison_boundaries: This cohort's ME/CFS prevalence (49%) must not be pooled with the 9.8%-15.4% prevalence the authors cite from other international PCC studies [9-11], because the authors themselves attribute the difference to recruitment bias toward severely affected, long-standing, occupationally disabled patients.

This cohort's multimorbidity rate (42%) must not be pooled with the 25.3% age-matched general-population rate cited from German/Swiss primary-care studies [46,47], as these represent different populations (occupational-disease-claim PCC cohort vs. general primary-care population) and possibly different multimorbidity definitions and measurement windows.

This cohort's VO2peak values (13.0-15.4 mL/min/kg in the severely affected occupational sample) must not be pooled with the population-based Peter et al. (2025) PCC-without-ME/CFS cohort (~27.9 mL/min/kg at 2 years post-infection), since these are structurally different populations (severity-selected occupational-disease claimants vs. a population-based sample), not alternate measurements of the same quantity.

All percentages and means reported here are specific to this single cohort (n=92, Mainz, Germany, enrolled July 2023-March 2025, 88% female, employed in healthcare/social-services sectors) and should not be extrapolated to the general PCC or ME/CFS population without an explicitly labeled assumption.

No dollar or cost figures of any kind appear in this document; nothing in it should be combined with cost data from other sources without separately establishing a matching price year, population, and cost perspective.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: Inclusion criterion 3 (Table 1) required that PCC diagnosis be established by a physician using ICD-10 code U09.9 as the main diagnosis; every patient in this cohort - and therefore every modeled_issues percentage derived from it (work disability rate, ME/CFS prevalence, PEM positivity, occupational status distribution, etc.) - was selected on the basis of already having received that diagnosis code, a claims/ICD-10-coded basis for cohort definition.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: Cohort-level percentages (66.3% objective work disability, 49% ME/CFS prevalence, 79% PEM positivity, 75%/12%/13% occupational status distribution, 48.9% Bell-Score ≤30) are each reported as a single pooled figure for the whole cohort, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status beyond ME/CFS classification, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, despite the cohort being 88% female.

spec.title: Long COVID Occupational Disability Cohort: CPET and Functional Status Findings (Mainz, Germany)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces percentages and counts reported for a single, severity-selected German occupational-disease cohort (n=92) of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients evaluated with cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET). It does not include any medical cost, wage, insurance-payment, or caregiver-cost data, because none are reported in the document. It should not be used to estimate PCC or ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome) prevalence or disability rates in the general population.

takeaway.patient: This study followed 92 people with long-lasting post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) in Germany who were being evaluated for work-related disability recognition, about half of whom also met criteria for ME/CFS. Using an exercise breathing test (CPET), the study found that 66.3 percent of this specific, severely affected group had objectively reduced oxygen uptake or power output, and this objective finding lined up with how disabled patients rated themselves and with their actual work status (75 percent on sick leave, 13 percent working, 12 percent in gradual return-to-work). Post-exertional malaise - a worsening of symptoms after physical or mental effort - was reported far more often among patients who also met ME/CFS criteria (93 percent) than those who did not (64 percent) in this sample. These findings describe this one severity-selected group of patients referred for occupational evaluation, not long COVID or ME/CFS patients generally.
takeaway.care: In this severity-selected German occupational-disease cohort (n=92), CPET-derived measures (VO2peak, peak power output) classified 66.3 percent of patients as meeting the study's objective work-disability threshold, and these objective measures correlated with self-reported disability (Bell Disability Scale) and with actual occupational status (75 percent sick leave, 13 percent working, 12 percent in reintegration). Post-exertional malaise positivity was markedly higher in the ME/CFS subgroup (93 percent) than the non-ME/CFS subgroup (64 percent, p=0.002). The authors frame CPET as a tool to supplement organ-centered diagnostics, which in this population frequently returned unremarkable results despite substantial functional impairment.
takeaway.policy: This is a clinical/occupational-medicine study, not a cost-of-illness analysis - it reports no dollar figures. In this severity-selected, occupationally-referred German cohort (n=92, 88 percent female, all carrying an ICD-10 U09.9 PCC diagnosis), 66.3 percent met CPET-based objective work-disability thresholds, 49 percent also met ME/CFS criteria (versus 9.8-15.4 percent in other cited PCC cohorts, a difference the authors attribute to this cohort's recruitment bias toward severe, long-standing, occupationally disabled cases), and 75 percent were on sick leave at evaluation. These rates describe only this specific, claims-selected, non-representative sample and have not been broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity despite the cohort's skewed composition.

patient: If standard organ-focused tests have come back normal but fatigue and post-exertional malaise (worsening after exertion) persist, you could ask your care team whether an objective exercise capacity test (CPET) might help document functional limits, since this study found such tests correlated with patients' own self-reported disability and actual work status.

If you notice your symptoms worsen after physical or mental effort, this study reported that pattern was common among similarly severely affected patients, especially those also meeting ME/CFS criteria - this may be useful context to describe clearly to your clinician.

This study describes a specific, severely affected German cohort referred for occupational-disability evaluation; its percentages should not be assumed to predict your own individual outcome or diagnosis likelihood.
care: Consider whether a CPET-based protocol (VO2peak, peak power output) alongside the Bell Disability Scale could supplement organ-centered diagnostics when standard organ-specific results are unremarkable in patients with persistent post-COVID symptoms and suspected work disability, as this study's authors suggest.

This study's stratification of occupational status (sick leave vs. reintegration vs. currently working) alongside CPET and Bell-Score findings may be worth reviewing as one reference point when structuring graded return-to-work discussions for similarly severely-affected patients.

Given the markedly higher post-exertional malaise rate in the ME/CFS subgroup found here (93 percent vs 64 percent), screening severely affected PCC patients against Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS before recommending exertion-based rehabilitation may be worth considering.

Note that this cohort was severity-selected, occupationally referred, and lacked a matched healthy control group per the study's own limitations; any protocol change inspired by these findings should account for possible non-generalizability.
policy: Occupational-disease and workers'-compensation evaluators designing disability-determination protocols for severe PCC/ME-CFS could review whether CPET-based thresholds alongside self-reported disability scales offer a useful, objective complement to current organ-centered evaluation criteria.

Because this cohort's ME/CFS prevalence and disability rates come from a severity-selected, occupationally-referred, ICD-10-coded sample, they should not be used as general-population PCC or ME/CFS prevalence or burden estimates without separate, representative data.

Commissioning a larger, multi-site study with a matched healthy control group and sex/age/race-disaggregated analysis (of the kind federal surveys such as NHIS and BRFSS typically support) would help determine whether these findings generalize beyond this single German occupational cohort.

Since no cost or insurance-payment data are reported in this document, it cannot itself support cost-effectiveness or budget-impact decisions for PCC/ME-CFS disability programs; cost data would need to be obtained separately.

inputs.label: Cohort size
inputs.source: Cohort size (n=92) reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 50-150 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total number of patients in this German occupational-disease PCC cohort; moving it tests how the count-based outputs below would scale for a similarly-selected cohort of a different size, without changing the cohort's observed percentages.

inputs.label: Objective work-disability rate (CPET-defined)
inputs.source: 66.3% reported in Conclusion, p.14; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's central finding: the share of the cohort meeting CPET-based thresholds (VO2peak <15 mL/min/kg and/or peak power output <1 W/kg) for objective work disability; moving it explores how sensitive the estimated patient count below is to this rate.

inputs.label: ME/CFS prevalence within cohort
inputs.source: 49% (45/92) reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported share of the cohort who also met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS; moving it changes the estimated ME/CFS subgroup count below, while keeping in mind the authors' caution that this rate is likely elevated relative to other PCC cohorts due to recruitment bias toward severity.

inputs.label: Post-exertional malaise positivity, ME/CFS subgroup
inputs.source: 93% reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported rate of post-exertional malaise (symptom worsening after exertion) among cohort patients who also met ME/CFS criteria; moving it changes the PEM-gap output below.

inputs.label: Post-exertional malaise positivity, non-ME/CFS subgroup
inputs.source: 64% reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported post-exertional malaise rate among cohort patients who did not meet ME/CFS criteria; moving it alongside the ME/CFS-subgroup rate shows how large a gap the study's data reflect between the two subgroups.

inputs.label: Share of cohort on medical sick leave
inputs.source: 75% (69/92) reported in Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported share of the cohort on medical sick leave at evaluation; moving it changes the occupational-status gap output below.

inputs.label: Share of cohort currently working
inputs.source: 13% (12/92) reported in Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported share of the cohort currently working despite PCC; moving it alongside the sick-leave rate shows how the gap between those unable and able to work would change in this cohort.

inputs.label: Share scoring ≤30 on Bell Disability Scale
inputs.source: 48.9% (of n=88 responders) reported in Results, Association Between CPET and Bell Disability Scale, p.10; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of Bell-Disability-Scale responders in this cohort scoring at or below 30 (moderate-to-severe self-reported disability on a 0-100 scale); moving it explores how the self-reported-disability share compares with the objective CPET-based work-disability rate above.

outputs.label: Estimated patients meeting objective work-disability threshold
outputs.interpretation: This estimates how many of the cohort patients met the study's CPET-based thresholds for objective work disability. The document reports 66.3% (61/92) met this threshold; a higher value means more of this specific cohort showed objectively reduced exercise capacity consistent with work disability, as observed in this sample, not a population-wide disability rate.

outputs.label: PEM positivity gap: ME/CFS minus non-ME/CFS subgroup (positive = ME/CFS subgroup higher; negative = non-ME/CFS subgroup higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between post-exertional malaise (symptom worsening after exertion) positivity reported for the ME/CFS subgroup (93%) and the non-ME/CFS subgroup (64%) within this same cohort, a difference the authors report as statistically significant (chi-square=9.6, p=0.002). A larger positive gap means PEM was reported notably more often among patients who also met ME/CFS criteria in this specific sample; this is an observed association in this cohort, not a causal claim.

outputs.label: Occupational-status gap: sick leave minus currently-working rate (positive = more on sick leave than working; negative = more working than on sick leave)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the share of this cohort on medical sick leave (75%) and the share currently working despite PCC (13%), both measured at the same evaluation point. A larger positive value means more of this specific cohort was unable to work than was working; it does not include the 12% reported to be in active occupational reintegration.

outputs.label: Self-reported moderate-to-severe disability share (Bell Scale ≤30)
outputs.interpretation: This reflects the percent of Bell-Disability-Scale responders in this cohort (a 0-100 self-reported functional-status scale where lower scores indicate greater disability) scoring at or below 30, a threshold the authors treat as moderate-to-severe disability. A higher value means more patients in this specific cohort rated their own functional capacity as severely limited; the document reports this self-reported measure correlated with the objective CPET findings.

outputs.label: Estimated patients meeting ME/CFS criteria
outputs.interpretation: This estimates how many of the cohort patients met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS (49%, 45/92) in addition to their PCC diagnosis. The authors note this prevalence is far higher than the 9.8%-15.4% reported in other PCC cohorts cited in the document, and they attribute that difference to this cohort's recruitment bias toward severely affected, long-standing, occupationally disabled patients rather than claiming it reflects true ME/CFS prevalence among PCC patients generally.

scenarios.label: Equalize subgroup PEM rates
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the reported PEM gap drives apparent ME/CFS-specific burden.
scenarios.description: Sets both ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS subgroup PEM positivity to the cohort's own overall observed rate of 79%, showing the subgroup gap collapses to zero if both groups shared that rate.

scenarios.label: Count reintegration as working
scenarios.goal: Tests how the occupational-status gap changes under a different category grouping.
scenarios.description: Recombines the cohort's own reported reintegration (12%) and working (13%) categories into a single working group of 25%, leaving the sick-leave share unchanged, to show how category definitions affect the sick-leave-minus-working gap.

scenarios.label: Less severity-selected case mix
scenarios.goal: Shows how the ME/CFS subgroup count would differ outside this referral cohort.
scenarios.description: Sets ME/CFS prevalence to an illustrative 15%, near the upper end of the international PCC-cohort range (9.8%-15.4%) the authors cite, instead of this severity-selected referral cohort's observed 49%, to show the subgroup count under a different, non-causal case-mix assumption.

package.documentation:
This simulator reproduces figures reported in a single clinical/occupational-medicine study of 92 patients with long-standing post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) recruited through a German Social Accident Insurance (BGW) occupational-disease pathway in Mainz, Germany, between July 2023 and March 2025. About half of the cohort also met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome). All figures are percentages or counts drawn directly from the study; no cost, wage, insurance-payment, or caregiver-cost data appear anywhere in the document, so none are modeled here.

**Inputs** come from the study's Clinical Profile and Occupational Status results (pages 7 and 10) and its Conclusion (page 14): the objective CPET (cardiopulmonary exercise test)-based work-disability rate (66.3%, using VO2peak <15 mL/min/kg and/or peak power output <1 W/kg thresholds), ME/CFS prevalence within the cohort (49%), post-exertional malaise (PEM, symptom worsening after exertion) positivity separately for the ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS subgroups (93% vs 64%), sick-leave and currently-working rates (75% and 13%), and the share scoring at or below 30 on the Bell Disability Scale (48.9%, a self-reported 0-100 functional-status measure). Cohort size (n=92) and all percentage defaults are observed values from the study; slider ranges beyond the observed defaults are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not reported ranges from the document.

**Outputs** compute cohort counts and gaps between reported rates (the PEM-positivity gap between ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS subgroups, and the gap between sick-leave and working rates), using only the study's own reported figures - no external benchmarks are combined in.

**Limitations.** All participants were required to already carry an ICD-10 code U09.9 PCC diagnosis as an inclusion criterion, so every percentage here describes only already-diagnosed, already-coded patients referred for occupational-disability evaluation; the figures likely do not capture undiagnosed or uncoded PCC/ME-CFS cases and should not be read as a complete count of burden. The cohort's pooled percentages (work disability, ME/CFS prevalence, PEM positivity, occupational status, Bell-Score) have not been broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity in this document, despite the cohort being 88% female; federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform it. Separately, the study describes a systemic gap in care: organ-centered clinical diagnostics (cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurological) frequently yielded unremarkable findings in these patients, leaving clinicians without an objective framework for assessing work capacity, which the authors argue CPET is needed to fill. Finally, the authors caution that this cohort's ME/CFS prevalence (49%) is far higher than the 9.8%-15.4% reported in other PCC cohorts cited in the study, attributing the difference to recruitment bias toward severely affected, long-standing, occupationally disabled patients rather than to a true difference in ME/CFS risk - this cohort's rates should not be pooled with general-population PCC estimates.

inputs.label: Cohort size
inputs.source: Cohort size (n=92) reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 50-150 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total number of patients in this German occupational-disease PCC cohort; moving it tests how the count-based outputs below would scale for a similarly-selected cohort of a different size, without changing the cohort's observed percentages.

inputs.label: Objective work-disability rate (CPET-defined)
inputs.source: 66.3% reported in Conclusion, p.14; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's central finding: the share of the cohort meeting CPET-based thresholds (VO2peak <15 mL/min/kg and/or peak power output <1 W/kg) for objective work disability; moving it explores how sensitive the estimated patient count below is to this rate.

inputs.label: ME/CFS prevalence within cohort
inputs.source: 49% (45/92) reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported share of the cohort who also met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS; moving it changes the estimated ME/CFS subgroup count below, while keeping in mind the authors' caution that this rate is likely elevated relative to other PCC cohorts due to recruitment bias toward severity.

inputs.label: Post-exertional malaise positivity, ME/CFS subgroup
inputs.source: 93% reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported rate of post-exertional malaise (symptom worsening after exertion) among cohort patients who also met ME/CFS criteria; moving it changes the PEM-gap output below.

inputs.label: Post-exertional malaise positivity, non-ME/CFS subgroup
inputs.source: 64% reported in Results, Clinical Profile, p.7; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported post-exertional malaise rate among cohort patients who did not meet ME/CFS criteria; moving it alongside the ME/CFS-subgroup rate shows how large a gap the study's data reflect between the two subgroups.

inputs.label: Share of cohort on medical sick leave
inputs.source: 75% (69/92) reported in Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported share of the cohort on medical sick leave at evaluation; moving it changes the occupational-status gap output below.

inputs.label: Share of cohort currently working
inputs.source: 13% (12/92) reported in Results, Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity, p.10; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the reported share of the cohort currently working despite PCC; moving it alongside the sick-leave rate shows how the gap between those unable and able to work would change in this cohort.

inputs.label: Share scoring ≤30 on Bell Disability Scale
inputs.source: 48.9% (of n=88 responders) reported in Results, Association Between CPET and Bell Disability Scale, p.10; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of Bell-Disability-Scale responders in this cohort scoring at or below 30 (moderate-to-severe self-reported disability on a 0-100 scale); moving it explores how the self-reported-disability share compares with the objective CPET-based work-disability rate above.

outputs.label: Estimated patients meeting objective work-disability threshold
outputs.interpretation: This estimates how many of the cohort patients met the study's CPET-based thresholds for objective work disability. The document reports 66.3% (61/92) met this threshold; a higher value means more of this specific cohort showed objectively reduced exercise capacity consistent with work disability, as observed in this sample, not a population-wide disability rate.

outputs.label: PEM positivity gap: ME/CFS minus non-ME/CFS subgroup (positive = ME/CFS subgroup higher; negative = non-ME/CFS subgroup higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between post-exertional malaise (symptom worsening after exertion) positivity reported for the ME/CFS subgroup (93%) and the non-ME/CFS subgroup (64%) within this same cohort, a difference the authors report as statistically significant (chi-square=9.6, p=0.002). A larger positive gap means PEM was reported notably more often among patients who also met ME/CFS criteria in this specific sample; this is an observed association in this cohort, not a causal claim.

outputs.label: Occupational-status gap: sick leave minus currently-working rate (positive = more on sick leave than working; negative = more working than on sick leave)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the share of this cohort on medical sick leave (75%) and the share currently working despite PCC (13%), both measured at the same evaluation point. A larger positive value means more of this specific cohort was unable to work than was working; it does not include the 12% reported to be in active occupational reintegration.

outputs.label: Self-reported moderate-to-severe disability share (Bell Scale ≤30)
outputs.interpretation: This reflects the percent of Bell-Disability-Scale responders in this cohort (a 0-100 self-reported functional-status scale where lower scores indicate greater disability) scoring at or below 30, a threshold the authors treat as moderate-to-severe disability. A higher value means more patients in this specific cohort rated their own functional capacity as severely limited; the document reports this self-reported measure correlated with the objective CPET findings.

outputs.label: Estimated patients meeting ME/CFS criteria
outputs.interpretation: This estimates how many of the cohort patients met Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS (49%, 45/92) in addition to their PCC diagnosis. The authors note this prevalence is far higher than the 9.8%-15.4% reported in other PCC cohorts cited in the document, and they attribute that difference to this cohort's recruitment bias toward severely affected, long-standing, occupationally disabled patients rather than claiming it reflects true ME/CFS prevalence among PCC patients generally.

scenarios.label: Equalize subgroup PEM rates
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the reported PEM gap drives apparent ME/CFS-specific burden.
scenarios.description: Sets both ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS subgroup PEM positivity to the cohort's own overall observed rate of 79%, showing the subgroup gap collapses to zero if both groups shared that rate.

scenarios.label: Count reintegration as working
scenarios.goal: Tests how the occupational-status gap changes under a different category grouping.
scenarios.description: Recombines the cohort's own reported reintegration (12%) and working (13%) categories into a single working group of 25%, leaving the sick-leave share unchanged, to show how category definitions affect the sick-leave-minus-working gap.

scenarios.label: Less severity-selected case mix
scenarios.goal: Shows how the ME/CFS subgroup count would differ outside this referral cohort.
scenarios.description: Sets ME/CFS prevalence to an illustrative 15%, near the upper end of the international PCC-cohort range (9.8%-15.4%) the authors cite, instead of this severity-selected referral cohort's observed 49%, to show the subgroup count under a different, non-causal case-mix assumption.
